hallucinations.claim: "Magnesium glycinate beats citrate because the glycine chelate lets the mineral survive stomach acid and use amino-acid transporters, giving better bioavailability"
hallucinations.why: Reference: glycinate vs citrate is mostly marketing; both absorb well and no trial shows glycinate works better for anxiety. This is the 'clinically better' trap stated as fact.

hallucinations.claim: "Citrate ... is largely an osmotic laxative and competes for intestinal transporters, so its anxiolytic benefit is less consistent"
hallucinations.why: No evidence that citrate's anxiolytic effect is less consistent; citrate is well absorbed. The transporter-competition mechanism is invented.

hallucinations.claim: "most studies use a chelated form such as magnesium glycinate for anxiety relief"
hallucinations.why: The anxiety trials mostly used magnesium oxide, lactate or Mg+B6 combinations, not glycinate; unsupported.

hallucinations.claim: "Heavy drinking may cause GI upset, especially with citrate, so glycinate's gentler profile may be preferable"
hallucinations.why: Unsourced pairing of alcohol and citrate GI effects; not a documented interaction.

what_went_wrong: The gpt-oss:20b draft copied the glycinate-beats-citrate marketing from the search results (stopanxiety, dlmethod, modernmetabolic blogs), and the merge wrapped it in made-up mechanism; it also opened by repeating the turn-1 dose instead of answering the new question.
great_answer_would: Answer the three questions in order: no known sertraline interaction (tell the prescriber), a few drinks is fine though heavy drinking depletes magnesium, and glycinate vs citrate is mostly marketing, so choose by how your gut handles it and by price.
notes: Sertraline and alcohol answers are broadly right. It never says to tell the prescriber. Saying glycinate is about 13% elemental is close (about 14%) and was not flagged.

hallucinations.claim: "Antiperspirants use aluminum salts to block sweat ducts, effectively stopping sweat from emerging. Antiperspirants significantly reduce sweat production, but they don't stop it entirely."
hallucinations.why: Contradicts itself within two sentences; the second is right.

hallucinations.claim: "Your body still makes the same sweat, but the mix of glands and the bacteria that live on you have shifted."
hallucinations.why: Stated as a diagnosis with no basis; the cause of a change could be meds, diet, fabrics, age or illness.

what_went_wrong: The search returned stress-sweat blogs, so the answer blames stress alone. It drifts into scalp odour and gives generic fixes. It misses meds (SSRIs), diet, synthetic fabrics, night-time aluminium chloride, benzoyl peroxide washes and the red-flag smells.
great_answer_would: Give one line on bacteria breaking down apocrine sweat, list the likely causes of a change (stress, meds, diet, polyester), give the fix stack (10-20% aluminium chloride at night, a benzoyl peroxide or chlorhexidine wash, cotton and hot washes), then the red-flag smells.
notes: The mechanism is right. The 99% water, about a litre a day and 3 million glands figures are roughly standard. It ends with a recap sentence the asker said to skip, and the scalp paragraph is off-topic.

hallucinations.claim: "There is no evidence that eating large portions of pizza specifically causes over-eating; the claim that large portions encourage excess calories is unsupported [8]"
hallucinations.why: The portion-size effect is one of the best-replicated findings in nutrition science, and the cited PMC portion-size review supports it. The critic's 'unsupported' note was turned into a false claim.
Overgeneralised; ordinary NY or Neapolitan pizza has little added sugar. Not a key driver.

what_went_wrong: The merge turned the ministral reviewer's 'UNSUPPORTED' note into a claim that the evidence is absent. The search returned junk (listicles, a Washington pizza guide, a Turkish app page), which led to an off-topic sulfite paragraph. The answer opens with negatives, not a direct verdict.
great_answer_would: Open with 'no, once or twice a week is fine', give the per-slice calories and sodium (~250-350 kcal, ~600-800 mg), and name the three things that make it worse (portion, processed meat, extra cheese) with the fixes, in under 150 words.
notes: The frequency advice (once or twice a week, 1-2 slices with a salad) and the sodium range are about right. Calories are missing entirely.

hallucinations.claim: "morning people arrive about 15 minutes early and feel more cheerful, lively, and alert"
hallucinations.why: A pop-press detail (HuffPost) with no study behind it, stated as a research finding.

hallucinations.claim: "teenagers' night-owl tendencies fade with age, which may explain why older adults are happier than younger ones"
hallucinations.why: A speculative causal link with no support.

hallucinations.claim: "no direct evidence links such routines to a permanent shift from night-owl to morning-type"
hallucinations.why: Leans into the 'you can't change it' trap. The 2019 Facer-Childs (Birmingham) study moved owls about 2 hours earlier in 3 weeks with light, fixed wake times and meal timing.

what_went_wrong: The search found pop-press stories and an off-topic alarm wake-up-task study, so the answer leaves out social jetlag and gives no shift protocol. The model's own knowledge did not fill the gap.
great_answer_would: Say it's half true: owls report more depressive symptoms, mostly from social jetlag. Then give a protocol (fixed wake time, morning bright light, dim evenings, early meals and exercise, optional 0.5 mg melatonin) with the realistic 1-2 hour shift.
notes: The 18% lower depression risk from half the recommended exercise matches a real 2022 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis, but it doesn't answer the question. The 36-participant wake-up-task study is irrelevant.

hallucinations.claim: "the 2026-approved electric head shavers are the Philips Head Shaver Pro and the Remington Balder Pro RX5"
hallucinations.why: '2026-approved' is an invented framing for one review site's picks, and the exact product names are unverified.

what_went_wrong: The pick (a #1-#2 buzz with short sides as the lowest maintenance, a shave as the sharpest) is right, but the warning against the horseshoe is weak. The answer spends its end on shaver brands and a Panasonic maintenance guide from the search results instead of beard and sunscreen advice.
great_answer_would: Pick a #1-#2 buzz all over (or a shave if he'll keep it up), say plainly that long sides with a bald top is the look to avoid, give the upkeep for each option in a line, and add the beard-balance and daily scalp-sunscreen tips.
notes: The guard sizes, the clipper frequency and the shave cadence with moisturiser and SPF are right. 'Buzz top with faded sides' is acceptable.

hallucinations.claim: "the EX Program ... can raise quit odds by up to 40 %"
hallucinations.why: No such figure is traceable. EX trials show modest gains, and 'up to 40%' looks invented.

hallucinations.claim: "This signals autonomy, a factor linked to higher quit success [1]" and "research links to reduced undermining behavior and better quit outcomes [1]"
hallucinations.why: Overclaims a family-intervention review that found mixed or weak evidence.

what_went_wrong: The search pulled in a pregnancy page and a Bible-on-nagging page, and the merge kept both as sections, so the answer has a pregnancy note and 'Biblical guidance' for a user who mentioned neither. It is about twice the requested length and lacks the withdrawal timeline and quitline.
great_answer_would: Give a short script he can say to his family (don't ask daily, snappiness is withdrawal, no smoking around me, no lecture if I slip), the withdrawal timeline (peaks days 3-7, cravings 3-5 minutes), a Sunday check-in he picks, and 'the patch and gum are part of the plan', in under 200 words.
notes: It has some good content: a check-in cadence he controls (Day 7 and Day 14), naming the NRT method, and specific requests. EX by Truth Initiative with Mayo Clinic is real. The 20-minute heart-rate claim is the standard CDC line but irrelevant here.
